newsitem.title: USA: Sprint results higher, but hurt by charges, costs.
newsitem.headline: Sprint results higher, but hurt by charges, costs.

text.p: Sprint Corp. Tuesday reported strong fourth-quarter and 1996 results, as consumers added more telephone lines and services and increased their long distance telephone usage.

But the telecommunications company's profits were eroded by charges that were slightly higher than expected, and heavy start-up costs for its Global One joint venture and Sprint PCS, its wireless division.
Sprint earned $245.3 million, or 57 cents a share, in the quarter ended Dec. 31, after a $60 million one-time charge related to litigation involving its long distance division.
In the year-ago period, Sprint lost $343.2 million, or 98 cents a share, after the local phone division recorded an $88 million one-time restructuring charge.
Net operating revenues edged up to $3.6 billion from $3.3 billion.
For full-year 1996, profits almost tripled to $1.18 billion from $395.3 million. Net operating revenues rose to $14.0 billion from $12.8 billion.
Sprint's long distance division saw revenues rise 12.3 percent to $2.16 billion in the fourth quarter, boosting operating income 27.4 percent to $257 million.
The consumer, business and wholesale segments of the long distance business each recorded double-digit growth in revenues and call volume.
Local telephone revenues grew 7.9 percent to $1.33 billion and operating income rose 12.4 percent to $334 million, Sprint said.
Access lines increased by 5.6 percent to more than 7.1 million in the quarter, Sprint said.

"Nearly one-third of the access lines we added in the quarter were for second-line service to existing customers to meet their lifestyle and data access needs," William Esrey, chairman of the Kansas City, Mo.-based company, said in a statement.
"Overall, more than 9 percent of our customers now have second lines into their homes."
Global One, a joint venture formed in January 1995 with Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom, lost $30.6 million in the fourth quarter, compared with a loss of $11.9 million in the 1995 period.
Losses at Sprint PCS, which began services about a year ago, jumped to $71.4 million from $18.9 million.
Sprint said it expects earnings per share to decline in 1997 due to increased investment, but the company said it is bullish about its prospects.

"We expect our earnings per share will decline in 1997 compared with 1996 levels, primarily due to the increased early-stage losses associated with Sprint Spectrum and our expansion into the competitive markets," Arthur Krause, chief financial officer, told analysts in a teleconference.

"Irrespective of this near-term earnings trend, we are very bullish about our prospects ... We currently see no impediments to this momentum and we are targeting double-digit volume and revenue growth for the full year of 1997."
Krause said Sprint expects long distance profit growth in the double digits in the first quarter and all of 1997.
He said, however, that first-quarter volume growth may slow slightly due in part to the lack of toll-free lines for the Internal Revenue Service, which in the past had a strong seasonal impact.
"This traffic has traditionally had a lower average yield, so the reported gap between minutes and revenues should narrow," Krause said.

He said he also expects Sprint's local telephone segment to post double-digit earnings growth in the first quarter, as demand for secondary telephone lines and "class services" such as call waiting and caller I.D. is growing.
Sprint's stock rose 50 cents to $40.75 on the New York Stock Exchange at midday.
